skip_reason: LEGO 1 of course - legitimate bare-debut exception per ralph-methodology.md

new_known: I'm going to speak Spanish at six this evening
new_target: Voy a hablar español a las seis de la tarde
why: Shows that this LEGO is a clock-time tail that attaches to a taught hour ('a las seis'), inside a first-person future frame the two siblings never use - they are both third-person/we.

new_known: Are you going to help me this afternoon?
new_target: ¿Vas a ayudarme esta tarde?
partner_legos: are you going to → vas a
why: Puts the time phrase into a question addressed to the learner's partner, where all three siblings are flat statements or bare infinitive fragments.

new_known: I need to improve as quickly as possible
new_target: Necesito mejorar lo más rápido posible
why: Attaches the adverbial to a new verb pair the siblings never touch - every existing BUILD hangs it on 'terminar' or 'aprender'.

new_known: It's easy to explain what I mean
new_target: Es fácil explicar lo que quiero decir
partner_legos: what I mean → lo que quiero decir
why: Extends the 'es fácil + infinitive' frame onto a long taught chunk, so the learner sees the adjective carrying a whole clause rather than a single verb.

new_known: It surprises me how you understand different words
new_target: Me sorprende cómo entiendes palabras diferentes
why: Completes the 'me sorprende cómo…' frame that sibling B04 leaves hanging, with a second-person verb and an object the sibling USE phrases never pair it with.

new_known: I can wait for you for a while
new_target: Puedo esperarte por un rato
why: Hangs the duration phrase off a waiting verb and a modal, where both siblings only ever attach it to 'doing this'.

new_known: I'd like to learn words in this language
new_target: Me gustaría aprender palabras en este idioma
why: Every sibling BUILD is a bare noun phrase with a modifier; this is the first one that puts 'palabras' in an object slot under a verb.

lego_known: why can't I remember what you said
lego_target: por qué no puedo recordar lo que dijiste
old_known: Why can't I remember what you said?
old_target: ¿Por qué no puedo recordar lo que dijiste?
new_known: Why can't I remember what you said last night?
new_target: ¿Por qué no puedo recordar lo que dijiste anoche?
why: Anchors the question to a past time word, which is the one time reference the siblings do not carry and the one that best fits a reported 'you said'.

new_known: It surprises me that you don't like
new_target: Me sorprende que no te guste
why: Shows the subjunctive chunk under a second matrix verb - every sibling and every USE phrase runs it under 'es raro' or 'pienso que es raro'.

new_known: I know it but I don't understand it yet
new_target: Lo sé pero no lo entiendo todavía
why: Gives the object pronoun twice across a contrast, including once under negation, where the siblings only show a single affirmative clitic.

new_known: It's more important to have a conversation
new_target: Es más importante tener una conversación
partner_legos: to have a conversation → tener una conversación
why: Plugs the comparative frame into a noun-carrying chunk rather than the bare verb 'hablar' of the one existing sibling.

new_known: I'm sorry, I was hoping it would happen earlier
new_target: lo siento, esperaba que pasara antes
why: Plugs the hoping-frame into an apology opener and a time adverb, neither of which any sibling row uses - the siblings all drill the object slot (algo / algo diferente / eso no era lo que).

new_known: You need to come on Sunday morning
new_target: necesitas venir el domingo por la mañana
partner_legos: on Sunday morning → el domingo por la mañana
why: Shows venir taking a bare infinitive complement after necesitas - every sibling hangs it off podré / no podré, so the learner has only ever seen one governing verb.

new_known: He'll be able to look for it in the office
new_target: podrá buscarlo en la oficina
partner_legos: in the office → en la oficina
why: Puts the office inside an actual action with a third-person future-ability frame; the four siblings only ever attach an article or possessive (la / en la / mi oficina).

new_known: I am not sure that we will finish in time
new_target: no estoy seguro de que terminemos a tiempo
why: Uses the seguro de que frame from sibling B04 with a real subjunctive clause the course has already taught, instead of stopping at 'de eso' as every sibling does.

new_known: I'd like a glass today
new_target: me gustaría un vaso hoy
why: Moves the glass off the past-tense 'tomé' that both siblings and all five USE phrases lean on, into a wanting frame plus a time word.

new_known: She said that she can come
new_target: dijo que puede venir
why: Gives 'dijo que' a present-tense complement; all four siblings and thirteen USE rows report in the imperfect (quería / conocía / era), so the learner has never seen the frame take anything else.

lego_known: what's that blue thing over there
lego_target: Qué es esa cosa azul de allí
old_known: What's that blue thing over there
old_target: Qué es esa cosa azul de allí
new_known: Do you mind telling me what's that blue thing over there?
new_target: ¿Te importa decirme qué es esa cosa azul de allí?
why: Adds a politeness opener the learner already owns; the siblings only ever front it with saber-verbs (quiero / sabes / me gustaría saber) or puedes decirme.

new_known: I want to know if you know my father
new_target: quiero saber si conoces a mi padre
why: Embeds the question inside a statement instead of leaving it as a bare question, which is the one shape all five siblings share.

new_known: the woman who's talking to my sister at the party
new_target: la mujer que está hablando con mi hermana en la fiesta
why: Changes who is being talked to - every existing sibling and USE row ends 'con tu amigo' - and adds a place tail, so the learner sees the relative clause as a slot rather than a fixed string.

new_known: you should continue to the left
new_target: deberías seguir a la izquierda
why: Attaches the direction to a verb of motion other than 'ir', which is the only verb any sibling or USE row pairs it with.

new_known: you asked if I went to that place
new_target: preguntaste si fui a ese lugar
why: Gives preguntaste a yes/no complement with 'si'; both siblings and all six USE rows drill only wh-complements (dónde / lo que).

new_known: I'm sure that we should stop
new_target: estoy seguro de que deberíamos parar
why: Feeds the frame a complement that is not 'estará' - both siblings and five of six USE rows complete it with estará bien / aquí / listo.

new_known: in my opinion they'll be bored
new_target: en mi opinión estarán aburridos
partner_legos: in my opinion → en mi opinión
why: Both existing BUILDs pair the future with 'listos'; this shows the same future carrying a different adjective, and puts a stance opener in front of it.

new_known: they have to decide next month
new_target: ellos tienen que decidir el mes que viene
partner_legos: next month → el mes que viene
why: Teaches that the obligation frame takes any taught infinitive and can be pinned to a time expression, instead of only 'venir' as the sibling BUILD does.

new_known: next to that person
new_target: al lado de esa persona
why: Shows 'al lado de' taking a person rather than a place or a thing, which the siblings ('la tienda', 'esto') never do, and does it without needing the de+el contraction.

new_known: the hope we have left is that they're not serious
new_target: la esperanza que nos queda es que no estén hablando en serio
partner_legos: we have left → que nos queda
why: Gives the subjunctive chunk a full noun-phrase trigger built from two taught pieces, rather than the bare conjunction openers ('pero', 'al menos') the siblings use.

new_known: I'm not planning to sleep right now
new_target: no pienso dormir ahora mismo
partner_legos: I'm not planning to → no pienso
why: Every existing phrase is a wanting/needing frame; this plugs the infinitive into a negative intention frame and adds a time anchor.

new_known: unfortunately you're going to pay for a new bed
new_target: desafortunadamente vas a pagar por una cama nueva
partner_legos: you're going to pay → vas a pagar
why: This LEGO only has a home after a paying verb, so the new teaching is the sentence-front adverb attaching to that whole frame — a partner none of the USE phrases use.

new_known: I'll call you to check if it hurts
new_target: te llamaré para comprobar si duele
why: Supplies the missing left-hand side: what you actually do in order to check, which no sibling BUILD or USE provides, plus a fresh 'si' complement.

new_known: whenever you feel crazy
new_target: siempre que te sientas loco
why: All three sibling BUILDs complete this LEGO with 'solo'; this shows the slot takes any state adjective the learner already has.

new_known: I wish they wouldn't play music any longer
new_target: ojalá no pusieran música por más tiempo
partner_legos: they wouldn't play → no pusieran música
why: Attaches 'por más tiempo' to a third-person wish rather than to the learner's own waiting or staying, which is all the siblings and USE phrases do.

new_known: I can tell you a little more about what it's like
new_target: puedo decirte un poco más sobre cómo es
partner_legos: a little more → un poco más
why: Turns the chunk round from asking to offering — every existing phrase is the learner wanting to know; this is the learner telling.

new_known: we would have driven along the main road
new_target: habríamos conducido a lo largo de la carretera principal
partner_legos: the main road → la carretera principal
why: Every other phrase for this participle is first-person singular 'habría'; this shows the same participle unchanged under a plural auxiliary, and gives it a route rather than a destination.

new_known: would you like to have tea without milk?
new_target: ¿te gustaría tomar té sin leche?
why: Builds the offer out of the drinks vocabulary just taught, and teaches the negative modifier 'sin' inside the offer, where the existing phrases only ever use 'con azúcar'.
